title: Born of Her Tapas
hookLine: a fruit with a shell you need a hammer for, a grandmother's Friday fast, and a tree born from the goddess's discipline
carry: tapas: even fortune grows from disciplined heat
tomorrow: who is Alakshmi, and why do families scrub before Diwali?

lines: A SHELL YOU NEED A HAMMER FOR.
cards: The bilva fruit does not look generous. It's round and greenish-gold, with a shell so hard that people crack it against a stone step or with the back of a cleaver.
Inside is a sticky, fragrant pulp that some families stir into a cool summer drink. It's the same tree whose leaves this path saw offered to Shiva.
You might expect a softer fruit for a goddess of abundance, a mango, maybe. But when the Sri Sukta names her tree, it names this one. And it says where the tree came from.

teach.b: Here's the line, in paraphrase. O you who are the color of the sun, from your tapas the lord of the forest was born: your tree, the bilva. May its fruits, by tapas, drive away the misfortunes within and without.

It means heat, and then the heat of discipline: effort, austerity, the steady fire of a hard practice. In the old stories, sages keep that fire burning in the forest, and gods win their boons with it.
And here's the surprise: the hymn gives tapas to Sri.
The goddess of fortune, gold and ease is the one whose discipline makes the tree grow. In this line, abundance isn't the opposite of effort. It comes out of it.
Then the tree. Lord of the forest is an old way of saying a great tree, and its fruits push away misfortune by tapas too. The outer misfortunes are easy to list: an empty purse, a roof that leaks.

The inner ones are harder; some readers hear confusion there, the habits that block a person from within. Now the teaching, because Hindus live it. Tapas runs all through the faith, even in Lakshmi's worship.
Many families keep a vrat for her, a vow: a Friday fast, since Friday is her day, or in the South the Varalakshmi vow, a day of fasting and worship for the goddess.
A small heat, kept on purpose, in the name of the one whose own tapas grew a tree.

how: The bilva tree is treated as sacred in Hindu worship, where its leaves are offered, and this verse is recited as part of the Sri Sukta in Lakshmi worship.

games.q: you're writing a hymn to the goddess of abundance and need to say where her sacred tree came from. what do you say?
o: it simply appeared, effortless, like all her gifts.
it was born from her tapas, her discipline.
a king planted it for her.
games.why: the Sri Sukta says the bilva was born from her tapas: in this line, abundance grows out of effort.

practice: Choose to stay still, really still, for the whole sit, even when something itches or the mind wants to wander: that's tapas at its smallest, staying a little longer than is comfortable.
When the mind wanders, bring it back; the bringing back is the practice. If you keep a fast or a vow, remember it now.
If you pray, you can offer the effort to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let the stillness be its own offering.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. A hymn that says the bilva tree was born from the goddess's own tapas, and asks its fruit to drive away misfortune within and without.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bilvaḥ, the bilva tree (bael), which the Sri Sukta calls hers, born from her tapas.

carryVoice: Your line: tapas, even fortune grows from disciplined heat. Her own tapas grew the bilva tree. See you tomorrow.
